items.bankTopic: The center of the universe: alkenes

expert.concept: Hydroboration-oxidation is the one hydration that is both anti-Markovnikov and syn: B and H add to one face in one step, then OH replaces B with retention.
reasoning: Name the target: OH on the less substituted alkene carbon (anti-Markovnikov) with the new H and OH on the same face (syn).
Only hydroboration does both: boron goes to the less hindered, less substituted carbon, and B and H add together in one four-center step.
H2O2 and NaOH swap B for OH with retention, so the new H on the methyl carbon and the OH end up cis, which puts OH and CH3 trans: trans-2-methylcyclopentan-1-ol.

misconceptions.pull: Oxymercuration is the hydration students remember for "no rearrangement", but it is Markovnikov: OH lands on the methyl carbon, giving 1-methylcyclopentan-1-ol.
Acid-catalyzed hydration goes through the tertiary cation, so it is Markovnikov and gives the tertiary alcohol with no face control.
HBr without peroxides is Markovnikov (tertiary bromide), and a tertiary bromide with NaOH eliminates or gives the tertiary alcohol, never the secondary one.
Acid hydration again: Markovnikov tertiary alcohol, and heat pushes the equilibrium back to the alkene (E1).

items.bankTopic: The only reaction in organic chemistry

expert.answer: Sodium amide, NaNH2 (the pKa of ammonia is about 38)
expert.concept: An acid-base reaction runs toward the weaker acid: a base deprotonates an acid only if its own conjugate acid has the higher pKa.
reasoning: Compare each base's conjugate acid with the alkyne's pKa of 25: the deprotonation goes only if that conjugate acid is weaker (higher pKa).
Ammonia (38) is far weaker than the alkyne, so amide pulls the proton and the equilibrium lies about 10^13 toward the acetylide.
Water and ethanol (16) are stronger acids than the alkyne, so hydroxide and ethoxide leave it almost untouched (K about 10^-9).

misconceptions.choice: Sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO3 (the pKa of carbonic acid is about 6)
misconceptions.pull: Reads the pKa scale upside down (low pKa as strong base); carbonic acid is far stronger than the alkyne, so bicarbonate cannot take its proton.

misconceptions.choice: Sodium acetate (the pKa of acetic acid is about 5)
misconceptions.pull: Same upside-down reading of the scale; acetate is a weak base whose conjugate acid is 20 pKa units stronger than the alkyne.

misconceptions.choice: Sodium hydroxide, NaOH (the pKa of water is about 16)
misconceptions.pull: "Strong base" from general chemistry pulls here, but water (16) is a stronger acid than the alkyne (25), so the equilibrium sits on the side of the alkyne.

misconceptions.choice: Sodium ethoxide, NaOEt (the pKa of ethanol is about 16)
misconceptions.pull: Ethoxide is the strong base used for E2 and enolates, so it feels strong enough; ethanol (16) is still the stronger acid, so the alkyne stays mostly protonated.

key.text: Sodium amide, NaNH2 (the pKa of ammonia is about 38)

checks.numbers: K = 10^(pKa of the base's conjugate acid - 25): ammonia 38 gives 10^13 (complete); water and ethanol 16 give 10^-9; carbonic acid 6 and acetic acid 5 give 10^-19 and 10^-20. One subtraction each, no calculator.

items.bankTopic: Reading the machines: spectroscopy, lab and synthesis

expert.answer: The O-H stretch is broadened and shifted to LOWER wavenumber (below ~3200 cm-1)
expert.concept: A hydrogen bond weakens the O-H bond, so its stretch moves to lower wavenumber, and the range of bond strengths broadens the band; a chelating intramolecular H-bond does this strongly.
reasoning: Picture the six-membered ring the phenol O-H closes onto the aldehyde O=C.
The H-bond pulls on the hydrogen and weakens the O-H bond; a weaker bond vibrates at lower frequency, so the band moves down.
A spread of H-bond strengths smears the band, so it is broad; chelated phenols like salicylaldehyde sit near or below 3200 cm-1, even in dilute solution.

misconceptions.choice: The O-H stretch becomes a sharp doublet, much like the two N-H bands of a primary aromatic amine
misconceptions.pull: Two bands belong to an NH2 group (symmetric and asymmetric stretches); one O-H has only one H, so there is no doublet.

misconceptions.choice: The O-H band moves to ~2250 cm-1, overlapping the nitrile region
misconceptions.pull: Around 2250 cm-1 is the triple-bond region (C-N and C-C triple bonds); an H-bond lowers the O-H stretch, but nowhere near that far.

misconceptions.choice: The O-H stretch sharpens and shifts to HIGHER wavenumber (above 3600 cm-1)
misconceptions.pull: Sharp and above 3600 cm-1 is a free, non-bonded O-H (dilute or gas phase); H-bonding moves the band the other way.

misconceptions.choice: The O-H stretch disappears entirely from the spectrum once the internal hydrogen bond forms
misconceptions.pull: The band shifts and broadens, sometimes into the C-H region, but the O-H bond is still there and still absorbs.

key.text: The O-H stretch is broadened and shifted to LOWER wavenumber (below ~3200 cm-1)

checks.numbers: Band positions (textbook): free O-H about 3600 cm-1 and sharp; H-bonded O-H broad and lower; chelated phenols like salicylaldehyde near or below 3200 cm-1; nitrile region about 2250 cm-1.

items.bankTopic: The alpha carbon wakes up

expert.concept: A Dieckmann closure is reversible; the ring that keeps an acidic H between the ketone and the ester gets deprotonated by ethoxide, and that last step pulls the equilibrium to it.
reasoning: Find the two alpha carbons: C2 (a CH carrying the methyl) and C5 (a CH2).
Both closures make a five-membered ring: the C5 enolate attacking the C1 ester puts the ketone between CH(CH3) and CH(CO2Et); the C2 enolate attacking the C6 ester makes a quaternary C(CH3)(CO2Et).

Ethoxide removes the doubly activated H between ketone and ester to drive the reaction; only the first product has one, so the quaternary product reopens and everything funnels to ethyl 3-methyl-2-oxocyclopentane-1-carboxylate.

misconceptions.pull: Same formula as the key, but the methyl carbon has been counted into the ring, giving a six-membered ring the chain cannot make.
The Dieckmann product of plain diethyl adipate; the methyl from the 2-position has gone missing.
The product of the 3-methyl isomer; here the methyl has slid to a ring carbon that touches neither carbonyl.
The other real five-membered closure; it forms, but with no H left between the carbonyls ethoxide cannot lock it in, so it reverts.

checks.numbers: RDKit ring sizes: key 5, choice with the methyl folded in 6, the three others 5. SMARTS check for an H on the carbon between ketone and ester: key yes, quaternary choice no (the Dieckmann driving step).

items.bankTopic: The switchboard: alcohols, ethers, epoxides

expert.answer: Benzaldehyde is reduced faster than acetophenone because the aldehyde carbonyl is less hindered and more electrophilic
expert.concept: Aldehydes beat ketones toward nucleophiles: one fewer electron-donating carbon group leaves the carbonyl carbon more positive, and the H leaves room for the incoming hydride.
reasoning: Compare what sits on each carbonyl carbon: benzaldehyde has phenyl and H; acetophenone has phenyl and methyl.
The methyl donates electron density (less partial positive) and crowds the carbon (and the tetrahedral intermediate), so hydride adds more slowly.
Both are reduced by NaBH4; the aldehyde simply goes first.

misconceptions.choice: Acetophenone is reduced faster because ketones are inherently more electrophilic than aldehydes at the carbonyl carbon in every solvent
misconceptions.pull: Turns the reactivity order around; ketones are the less electrophilic of the two.

misconceptions.choice: Both are reduced at identical rates because NaBH4 reacts only with esters
misconceptions.pull: Turns NaBH4's selectivity around: it reduces aldehydes and ketones and is too mild for most esters (LiAlH4 is the ester reducer).

misconceptions.choice: Neither reacts because NaBH4 cannot reduce conjugated aryl carbonyls
misconceptions.pull: NaBH4 does leave the aromatic ring and isolated C=C alone; that is true of those groups, not of the conjugated C=O, which it reduces.

misconceptions.choice: Acetophenone is reduced faster because the extra methyl group donates electron density that makes the carbonyl a better hydride acceptor
misconceptions.pull: The methyl does donate electron density, but donation makes the carbonyl carbon less positive, a worse hydride acceptor.

key.text: Benzaldehyde is reduced faster than acetophenone because the aldehyde carbonyl is less hindered and more electrophilic

items.bankTopic: The four questions: substitution and elimination

expert.concept: A carbocation next to a strained ring expands it (cyclobutylcarbinyl to cyclopentyl), and E1 loss of a proton then gives the most substituted alkene (Zaitsev).
reasoning: Protonate the OH and lose water: a secondary cation on the carbon next to the four-membered ring.
Shift a ring C-C bond onto that carbon: the ring grows from four to five atoms (strain falls from about 26 to about 6 kcal/mol) and the charge moves onto a ring carbon.
A 1,2-hydride shift makes the tertiary 1-methylcyclopentyl cation; losing a proton gives the trisubstituted alkene, 1-methylcyclopentene.

misconceptions.pull: Water can trap the rearranged tertiary cation as 1-methylcyclopentan-1-ol, but the stem asks for the alkene.
Eliminates before the ring expands; the stem says the shift happens first, and the four-membered ring keeps its strain.
The least substituted alkene with no shift, the kind of product a bulky base gives in E2; acid-driven E1 rearranges and goes Zaitsev.
Counts the methyl into the ring; one ring bond migrates, so the ring grows by one carbon (four to five), and the methyl stays outside.

expert.concept: An aldehyde plus two equivalents of alcohol under acid goes hemiacetal, then oxocarbenium ion, then acetal; excess alcohol (and loss of water) drives it to the acetal.
reasoning: Protonate the C=O and add one methanol: the hemiacetal.
Protonate its OH, lose water to the oxocarbenium ion, and add the second methanol.
Two OCH3 groups on the old carbonyl carbon: 1,1-dimethoxypropane, an acetal.

A methyl ester sits one oxidation level above the aldehyde; it needs the acid (Fischer esterification) or an oxidant, not just methanol.
The hemiacetal is the first adduct; with excess methanol and acid it goes on to the acetal.
Propanol needs a hydride source such as NaBH4; methanol and acid do not reduce the aldehyde.

items.bankTopic: Different arrows: radicals and Diels-Alder

expert.concept: Br2 with light is a radical chain that picks the weakest C-H; the benzylic C-H gives a resonance-stabilized radical, so Br lands on the benzylic carbon.
reasoning: Read the conditions: Br2 with light (no FeBr3) means radical substitution, not ring bromination.
Rank the C-H bonds: benzylic is weakest because its radical spreads into the ring.
Bromine selects strongly, so Br goes on the carbon attached to the ring: 1-bromo-1-phenylpropane.

misconceptions.pull: Ring bromination is EAS, which needs a Lewis acid (Br2, FeBr3); light starts a radical reaction on the side chain.
Puts Br at the end carbon, whose primary C-H is the strongest and gives the least stable radical: the ranking turned around.
Para bromination is the EAS answer for an alkyl benzene with Br2 and FeBr3; light changes the mechanism.
A secondary radical is decent, but it is not benzylic, so it loses to the radical next to the ring.

expert.concept: A neopentyl carbon is blocked for SN2 by the tert-butyl group next to it; in strong acid, water leaves with a 1,2-methyl shift, giving a tertiary cation that bromide traps.

A chloride needs HCl (with ZnCl2); this flask has only HBr, and the skeleton is unrearranged as well.
Primary alcohol plus HBr usually means SN2 with no rearrangement; neopentyl is the exception, because the tert-butyl blocks the back side.

items.bankTopic: The ring that refuses: aromatics

expert.answer: Deactivating but ortho/para directing; the acyl group enters mainly para
expert.concept: Halogens are the exception in EAS: inductive pull deactivates the ring, but a lone pair donated by resonance stabilizes the ortho and para sigma complexes; the bulky acylium prefers para.
reasoning: Split the two effects: induction (Br pulls electron density, slows EAS) and resonance (a Br lone pair stabilizes attack ortho and para).
Induction wins on rate (deactivating), resonance wins on position (ortho/para).
The acylium ion is bulky, so the crowded ortho position loses and the para product dominates.

misconceptions.choice: Activating and meta directing; the acyl group enters mainly meta
misconceptions.pull: Both halves turned around: bromine slows EAS and directs ortho/para.

misconceptions.choice: Deactivating and ortho/para directing; the acyl group enters mainly ortho only
misconceptions.pull: The classification holds, but ortho is crowded next to Br and the acylium is bulky, so para is the main product.

misconceptions.choice: Deactivating and meta directing; the acyl group enters mainly meta
misconceptions.pull: The usual rule (deactivators direct meta) applied to the one class that breaks it.

misconceptions.choice: Activating and ortho/para directing; the acyl group enters mainly para
misconceptions.pull: Direction and position hold, but the ortho/para label does not make bromine activating; it still slows the ring down.

key.text: Deactivating but ortho/para directing; the acyl group enters mainly para

expert.concept: Gilman cuprates are soft nucleophiles: they add 1,4 (conjugate addition) to an enone, putting the R group on the beta carbon; workup protonates the enolate and the ketone returns.
reasoning: Mark the enone: C=O, alpha carbon, beta carbon (the one carrying phenyl).
Me2CuLi adds methyl to the beta carbon (1,4), making an enolate.
Water protonates the alpha carbon; the C=O is back: 4-phenylpentan-2-one.

misconceptions.pull: 1,2-addition to the C=O is what MeLi or MeMgBr do; the cuprate goes 1,4.
Methyl is on the right carbon, but conjugate addition uses up the C=C; nothing puts it back.
Methyl on the alpha carbon is what an enolate plus CH3I gives; the cuprate attacks the beta carbon.
The cuprate leaves the ketone alone and the workup is only water; reducing the C=O needs a hydride.

expert.concept: A Cope rearrangement breaks the C3-C4 sigma bond, makes a new C1-C6 bond and shifts both pi bonds; it is reversible, so it settles on the isomer with the alkene conjugated to the ring.
reasoning: Number the diene 1 to 6: C1=C2, C3 (carries phenyl), C4, C5=C6.
Break C3-C4, join C1-C6, move the pi bonds to C2=C3 and C4=C5.

One pi bond moved, but the sigma bond did not break and the other pi bond stayed put; a [3,3] shift moves all three.
The six-membered ring belongs to the chair-like transition state (and to Diels-Alder products); the Cope product is still open chain, and this choice has lost two H.

The stereocenter's four bonds are untouched, so the drawing keeps the methyl on the same wedge.
Check the label: CH2NH2 (N,H,H) beats phenyl (C,C,C) at N, so the priority order is unchanged and the product is (S)-2-phenylpropan-1-amine (RDKit: S).

misconceptions.pull: The mirror image (R): nothing in the reaction touches the stereocenter, so nothing inverts.
Adds a methyl to the ring; no reagent here brings a carbon.
misconceptions.display: amine with an extra ring methyl

misconceptions.pull: An aldehyde is a partial reduction (DIBAL-H on an ester or nitrile); LiAlH4 on an amide goes all the way to the amine.
LiAlH4 on an ester or acid gives a primary alcohol; an amide keeps its nitrogen and gives an amine.
